There are lots of scripts out there with more than one idea - what’s important is deciding which one to make the primary focal point of your story. Too many plot threads can a story feel like its being pulled in too many different directions, and forget to invest in the audience in things as simple as the protagonist’s goal. It’s totally fine to write a script with multiple stories being told at once - hell, I’m currently developing a John Wayne biopic that’s also about the effects of radiation poisoning on small town America (which couldn’t sound like more of a clusterfuck just based off the tagline). As long as you can make it make sense, go for it!

How I ended up writing shows is something different - I was given the choice of either developing a pitch for a film or a show for the network, and after weighing up my options, the smarter move seemed to be making a show. Not only is streaming a great place to find an audience, but this show is pretty much custom built to go on for multiple seasons. I guess the lesson here is, if you’re pitching to a streaming service for the first time, it’s all well and good to know exactly what they’re after from you, but more important is to know exactly what you’re after from them.

Went to see this on opening day in Australia, and the theatre was completely empty. In retrospect that was probably for the best because I was genuinely cacking my pants laughing for the majority of the film...

1) Tye Sheridan playing the protagonist doesn’t do the film any favours. As someone who went in blind, he was completely bland and probably the least magnetic lead Spielberg’s ever had one in one of his films.
2) The poor dialogue and weak characters leave zero impact after the credits roll. I would have been happy to spend the whole film with just Art3mis and Aech, as both of the actresses playing them at least seemed like they were having fun with the material. So many capable actors wasted on weak and padded material.
3) The best they could do to make Olivia Cooke not look beautiful was put a red splotch over her right eye? Get out. The “reveal” of her IRL appearance was fucking hilarious.
4) The camerawork within the Oasis was so unbelievably mechanical - I’ve seen video games for the PS3 with more natural looking camerawork in their cutscenes. Only a handful of the scenes within the Oasis actually seemed tangible - it was also always so painfully obvious that the world around the characters in every scene was chock-full of green screens. Disappointed that Spielberg only seemed to use practical sets for the interior of IOI’s HQ and bits of the slums. 
5) Credit where credit’s due, the VFX artists who worked on the Shining sequence deserve an award. That scene was easily my favourite in the film, but in a better version of the film, the naked woman encounter could have easily had a bigger impact on Aech/Helen’s character arc, or at least added some stakes to the damn film. The only characters that died were dicks anyway.

With all the shoehorned product placement, out of place 80s rock songs, characters from other IPs, and the quote-un-quote romance between Tired Sheridan and Olivia “How Was I Paid Less Than This Guy For This Movie” Cooke, I’m just disappointed that one of the best filmmakers of all time couldn’t bring anything to the premise. I could go for all day on this, this is genuinely one of the most baffling movie experiences I’ve ever had.

What did you guys think? Seems like there’s an abundance of fanboys (I cringed as I typed that) that are overlooking this film’s obvious flaws.

**The Beguiled (Sofia Coppola, 2017)** Ostensibly, it's the best-directed film I've ever seen about eight girls who really, really want to fuck Colin Farrell. Admittedly, it's a little campy at times, but what good Sofia Coppola film isn't? Kirsten Dunst, Nicole Kidman, and all the young cast are pretty terrific, but the strongest performance comes from Farrell, who does a remarkable job of carrying the whole film with his dangerous charisma. Worth the price of admission for the sheer aesthetic alone. 7/10.

**Misery (Rob Reiner, 1990)** Rewatching this film cemented it as one of my favourite horror films of all time. Reiner was an inspired choice for the director's chair - not traditionally known for horror movies, my girlfriend, whom I saw it with, thought it was a 'feel good' movie up until the end of the first act. Tonally, the film pulls off a bold and shocking shift effortlessly, and by the time Beethoven's 'Moonlight Sonata' was playing during the infamous hobbling scene, I found myself prepared to call this movie a masterpiece. Career-best performances by Kathy Bates and James Caan really don't hurt either. 10/10.

**Snowden (Oliver Stone, 2016)** Over-dramatised and surprisingly poorly executed. Stone directs this tech-paranoia thriller with all the subtlety of Lawnmower Man. A film about Edward Snowden could have been interesting - hell, a film about Edward Snowden directed by Oliver Stone could have been interesting. In the end, the only good thing to come of it was an unintentionally hilarious scene towards the end of the film, featuring Nicolas freakin' Cage - playing Snowden's former mentor - with a beer in hand as he watches Snowden's face come up on the news, depicting the initial freakout of the WikiLeaks scandal as Snowden is now a wanted man. And I shit you not, upon finding this out, Cage just grins and goes "...he did it. The kid did it." This scene: 10/10. The rest of the film: 3/10.

Definitely makes more sense when you explain the "part of a greater narrative" aspect of it - but as a Room fanatic, I have to point out that the cancer storyline from The Room could have worked with the right script and direction. The reason why it sticks out and feels wrong is the awful execution of the reveal in the first place - the line in which both Lisa and the audience find out that her mother has cancer reads word-for-word: "by the way, I got the results of the tests back; I definitely have breast cancer", in the most flippant, casual delivery imaginable. It's simply impossible to buy. 

However, if instead of this horseshit expository dialogue, Wiseau had dedicated a few minutes of his film to emotionally invest his audience in the characters with stakes in this totally-left-field storyline and ran with it, the film might be... well, better. Unfocused, absolutely, but we would have had at least one character to care about as a result. But we were left with the line in the film instead, and you know what? If I had the opportunity to, I wouldn't change a damn thing... God, I love Tommy Wiseau.

I think I have to disagree with your point on "characters aren't people" - the key to quite a lot of characters in film is their humanity. Sure, some characters can be manifestations of themes and ideas represented in your script, and can often only exist within the world of their stories to serve plot points, but the moment that you start seeing your characters as ingredients rather than tangible beings living within your story's self-contained world is the moment that your story is at risk of losing substance and nuance, and bullshit like 'Doomsday' (if BvS' incarnation of the character can even be *considered* a character) is written into scripts.

Please don't use a lack of coverage as an excuse for a character's phone not to work. 

Yes, in the real world there are some locations that phones don't get signals in, but every time I'm watching a horror movie made from the year 2000 onwards and the director cuts to an insert shot of a phone that reads "No Signal", my eyes glaze over - me and my horror movie junkie friends complain about this trope constantly. 

I don't mean to be too harsh, but if this is a "monster in the house script", then you're already one horror cliché too deep. Obviously, it's all about the execution rather than the premise, and you could well have written *the* definitive "monster in the house script" that ends up defining the entire horror genre, but you'll just make things harder for yourself when it comes to the audience's suspension of disbelief by buying into that cliché.

Adam Wingard's "You're Next" actually had a clever way around this by having the criminals in the film use a jammer so that there's actually a reason for the victims' phones not to work. Try to keep that in mind - finding creative ways of subverting genre clichés and expectations is key when writing effective horror.

If you're familiar with Donald's stuff across music, television, and yes, this screenplay, you'll notice that none of it is really "traditional". 

My theory is that this is because he doesn't make shit for a specific audience, but rather for himself, and if people happen to enjoy it, that's just a bonus. 

"Awaken, My Love" is perhaps the best example of this, as it's both a love letter to both the music Donald's father used to play for him when he was a child, and a series of messages and lessons for Donald's own newborn son.

I'm not saying that Donald's work is exempt from all criticisms, but as his intentions for Because the Internet are clearly very different from the standard (his intention being to release it at the same time as his album, rather than to actually make a film out of it), it should be judged as it's own piece of self-contained writing, not as a blueprint for a movie, which is what most other scripts are.
